### Summary
Antarctic krill (*Euphausia superba*) is a keystone species of the Southern Ocean, supporting one of the world's largest fisheries and forming the foundation of food webs that sustain penguins, seals, and whales. Yet krill populations fluctuate strongly from year to year, with recruitment success depending on a tightly coupled interplay between ocean currents and sea ice. KRICO uses Lagrangian particle tracking, forced by three decades of high-resolution ocean reanalysis, to follow the dispersal of billions of virtual larvae between spawning grounds and overwintering habitats across the southwest Atlantic and Amundsen sectors. The simulations resolve when and where successful recruitment occurs, what causes it to fail, and how these patterns differ between regions exposed to opposite directions of sea-ice change. Results inform the spatial management of the krill fishery by the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR), and establish the baseline needed to anticipate how krill populations will respond to continued climate change toward 2050–2100.

### Approach
The hindcast covers 32 spawning seasons (1994–2025) across CCAMLR Subareas 48.1–48.6 and 88.3. Every day from mid-November to mid-March, about 546,000 virtual larvae are released along the continental slope (1000–2000 m depth) and tracked for 200 days with [Parcels](https://parcels-code.org), forced by the GLORYS12v1 ocean reanalysis at 1/12° resolution. In total, the simulations follow more than 2.1 billion trajectories from 3,848 daily cohorts, run on the ECMWF high-performance computing facility. Each larva is then classified as recruited, if it reaches the furcilia IV stage over the shelf or slope before the local winter sea-ice advance, or assigned to one of several failure modes linked to sea ice, larval development and transport.

### First results
Recruitment success peaks for larvae released in late January, and sea ice sets the window at both ends. Earlier in the season, sea ice still covers much of the spawning habitat. Later in the season, larvae no longer have time to complete their development before the winter sea-ice advance. The balance between these two constraints differs from one region to another, which produces marked regional asymmetries in recruitment. A second study, on the interannual variability of recruitment and its links with large-scale climate modes, is in progress.

Van de Putte, Timing of sea-ice retreat and advance governs the January peak and regional asymmetries in Antarctic krill larval recruitment, *ESS Open Archive* (preprint). - [krico-post-production](https://github.com/ogourgue/krico-post-production): recruitment classification pipeline. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22878123)
- [krico-paper1](https://github.com/ogourgue/krico-paper1): figure and analysis scripts for the first paper. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22878156)
